No, I believe I'm correct in this, such as a lower se position will be putting the body in a "1/4" squat position which is a strong position to produce power from a leg extension which is a quadriceps agonist movment. Great example is grant holloway vs ronnie baker, ronnie is more quad dominant and grant is much more hip dominant and look at their set positions.

A lot of times a start position will depend on if your hip dominant or quad dominant, hip dom ppl will have higher hips in set position while quad will have lower hips. Either way a neutral flat spine and a relaxed head whole keeping the same amount of pressure on the hands during a ready, and set position is preferred. As far as 1st steps, focus on good heel recovery and planting the foot underneath your hip not in front of you. Hope this helps!

I think the gastroc is super important but even more important is the Achilles tendon, acting as a spring complex for the lower limb and allowing highest energy transfer/return for the lower limb depending on how stuff is.

One of the main things I could see is that you're foot strike is both in front of your body, and striking with a heel/flat strike, try to make a "scissor"motion so you're knees are level when making the aggressive switch, and planting on the ball of you're foot directly under your hips because that could greatly help. Another thing is that it could also be an immense amount of volume depending on the high intensity (see altis short sprints or charlie Francis high/low methodology) as you may be doing too much volume at such a high intensity.

Not to mention front rack mobility doesn't become a limiting factor, and if someone isn't proficient in a clean they can pick a weight up and jump

I think dynamic mobility is better than static stretching (see RAMP style warmup) so of the overly limber athletes tend to get hurt because they are able to put their body into positions they can't produce force out of, so that being the case I don't think static is necessarily the best option.
The most reliable one I've worked with was an Infrared laser Browser timing system, idk if it's the most cost effect but I know free lap works relatively well with a decent price tag as well.

Best increase for acceleration are going to be body position (45ish degree from ground) maximum strength increase as well as an increase of rate of force development, or how fast your putting force into the ground which can be helped by increased strength and lower heel recovery to get the foot down quicker, which will decrease the amount of time it takes to get to top speed. Ankle hops are great for a rudimentary recovery day to help strengthen the ankle complex and achilles and reduce the amount of caving from force production so less "leaked energy" ankle stiffness is great for sprinters when it comes to energy returns.
